A.notes: Covers the central comparison, contest tools, accessible explanations, step-by-step examples, and mathematical correctness. Omits diagrams, acronym expansion, contest formats, and problem-source checks. Several synthesis criteria substantially overlap.

B.notes: Strongest treatment of theorem conditions, worked reasoning, strategic tool selection, curricular variation, and contest-format distinctions. Mostly observable criteria with useful factual-error safeguards. Still misses diagrams and their placement, explicit acronym expansion, early theorem placement, and problem citations.

C.notes: Captures the core contrast, audience, unfamiliar tools, and a worked problem. The blanket prohibition on solutions relying on school-taught tools is overbroad and conflicts with building contest reasoning from familiar foundations. Missing broad correctness safeguards and several reference obligations; negatively labelled criteria also use ambiguous negated phrasing.

D.notes: Provides substantial comparison, terminology guidance, non-routine techniques, and solution steps. Repeated comparison and audience criteria reduce atomicity. Mandatory auxiliary-construction and advanced-topic coverage adds unnecessary scope, while claims about curricular absence and time pressure need calibration. Mathematical and competition-fact error checks are incomplete.

decision_notes: B best combines reference coverage with precise, teachable, and judgeable expectations. A exceeds D through stronger correctness safeguards and less prescriptive scope. C's overbroad restriction on familiar tools is a substantial weakness. All four omit important diagram, presentation, and problem-source obligations.
